lesson.title: Hexadecimal
lesson.objective: Convert between binary, hexadecimal and denary without notes, and explain why programmers use hexadecimal.

vocabulary.meaning: A base 16 number system that uses the digits 0 to 9 and the letters A to F, where A to F stand for 10 to 15.
A group of 4 bits. One hex digit represents exactly one nibble, so one byte is two hex digits.

misconceptions.wrong: Writing a number in hexadecimal makes it take up less storage space.
misconceptions.correction: The computer only ever stores binary. Hex is a shorthand for people, so the number uses exactly the same number of bits.

misconceptions.wrong: When converting binary to hex, split the bits into nibbles starting from the left.
misconceptions.correction: Split into nibbles from the right and pad the left with 0s. For example, 10110 is 0001 | 0110, which is 16, not B0.

steps.note: Retrieval: architecture, binary and negative numbers

questions.q: State one difference between von Neumann and Harvard architecture.
questions.a: Von Neumann: one shared memory and bus for instructions and data. Harvard: separate memories and buses.

questions.q: State one reason why a RISC processor might be chosen instead of a CISC processor.
questions.a: Simple one-cycle instructions, so pipelining is easier and it uses less power.

questions.label: EXT
questions.q: State the range of denary values an 8-bit number can represent using sign and magnitude, and using two’s complement. Explain why the ranges are different.
questions.a: Sign and magnitude: −127 to +127. Two’s complement: −128 to +127. Sign and magnitude wastes a pattern on a second zero (10000000).

steps.heading: Why do we use hexadecimal, and how do we convert between hexadecimal, binary and denary?
steps.say: Write today’s date and the learning question at the top of your page.

steps.heading: 1.4.1 Data types
points: What we have learnt: binary and denary, binary addition, sign and magnitude, and two’s complement.
What we are learning: hexadecimal digits 0 to F, converting binary to hex and hex to binary, converting hex to denary and denary to hex, and why we use hex.
End goal: convert between binary, hex and denary without notes, and explain why programmers use hex.

steps.heading: Why hex? The problem
steps.say: Read this out loud, then copy it down: 110100111011111000101101. The same value written in hexadecimal is D3BE2D. That is 24 binary digits or 6 hex digits. Which would you rather copy without a mistake?

steps.heading: Hexadecimal digits
steps.say: Hex is base 16, so it has 16 digits. After 9, the letters A to F stand for 10 to 15. Each hex digit is exactly one 4-bit nibble.
points: 0 to 9 are the same as in denary: 0 is 0000 and 9 is 1001.

steps.heading: Hex is for humans
points: The computer only ever stores binary. Hex is a shorthand for people: it does not save any storage space.
One hex digit is exactly 4 bits (one nibble), so one byte is two hex digits: 1011 0110 = B6.
You will see hex in colour codes such as #FF8800, in MAC addresses and in memory addresses.

steps.heading: Choosing the letters
steps.say: In the 1950s, each computer used its own symbols for the values 10 to 15. IBM used 0 to 9 and A to F, and that became the standard we use today.
points: ILLIAC I (1952): K S N J F L
Bendix G-15 (1956): u v w x y z
LGP-30 (1956): F G J K Q W

steps.heading: Hexadecimal place values
steps.say: Each place is worth 16 times the place to its right. From the right, the place values are 1, 16 and 256 (16 × 16).

steps.heading: Binary to hexadecimal
points: 1. Split into nibbles from the right. Pad the left with 0s.
2. Convert each nibble to denary using 8, 4, 2, 1.
3. Write each value as one hex digit (10 to 15 = A to F).

points: 1. Write the place values 16 and 1 above the digits.
2. Multiply each digit by its place value.
3. Add the results.

steps.heading: Denary to hexadecimal
points: 1. Divide by 16. The whole number is the 16s digit.
2. The remainder is the 1s digit.
3. Or: convert to 8-bit binary, then split into nibbles. Both methods are accepted.

points: 1. Same rules: 12 bits = 3 nibbles, so 3 hex digits.
2. Three hex digits use the place values 256, 16 and 1.
3. Multiply and add, as before.

questions.label: A
questions.q: A student converts 10110 to hexadecimal and writes B0. What did they do wrong?
questions.a: 16. They grouped from the left. Group from the right: 0001 | 0110 → 1, 6.

questions.label: B
questions.q: Which is larger: 9F or A0? Explain how you know.
questions.a: A0. A0 = 160 and 9F = 159. The 16s digit decides: A is bigger than 9.

Convert the hexadecimal number FF to denary. In the Working column, explain why it is the largest value two hex digits can hold.
tasks.answer: 255 (15 × 16 + 15 = 255). F is the largest hex digit, so FF has both places at their maximum. It is the same value as 11111111, the largest 8-bit number.

Explain why programmers write bit patterns in hexadecimal rather than in binary.
tasks.answer: Hex is shorter, so it is easier for people to read, write and remember, and fewer mistakes are made. Each hex digit is exactly 4 bits, so it converts to and from binary quickly. 1 mark: shorter / easier to read. 1 mark: one hex digit = one nibble.

tasks.task: A student says: “Writing a number in hexadecimal makes it take up less storage space.” Explain why the student is wrong.
tasks.answer: Hex is only how people write the value. The computer still stores the number in binary, so it uses exactly the same number of bits. 1 mark: computers store binary, not hex. 1 mark: the number of bits is unchanged.

tasks.task: Describe the steps to convert a byte of binary into hexadecimal. Use an example alongside your explanation.
tasks.answer: Split the byte into two nibbles of 4 bits. Convert each nibble to denary using 8, 4, 2, 1. Write each value as one hex digit, using A to F for 10 to 15, in the same order as the nibbles. Example: 10110110 → 1011 | 0110 → 11, 6 → B6. 1 mark: split into two nibbles. 1 mark: each nibble becomes one hex digit, including A to F. 1 mark: a correct worked example.
